key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN onset during trauma - fall, twisting, or direct blow. LOCATION: Lateral malleolus (most common), medial malleolus, or posterior malleolus. DURATION: Immediate severe pain that persists. CHARACTER: SEVERE, SHARP, CONSTANT pain. AGGRAVATING: ANY weight bearing, ankle movement. RELIEVING: IMMOBILIZATION, ice, elevation, NSAIDs. TIMING: Immediate severe pain that persists until immobilization. SEVERITY: 7-10/10, severe and unrelenting. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: SWELLING within hours, BRUISING develops over 24-48 hours, DEFORMITY, inability to bear weight, numbness/tingling in foot (peroneal nerve compression). May have audible 'snap' or 'crack' at injury. KEY POSITIVES: Bony tenderness over fracture site, deformity, swelling, limited range of motion, positive compression test. KEY NEGATIVES: No open wound (rules out open fracture), no crepitus unless severe.

red_flags: Open wound with bone visible - open fracture, call 911
Severe deformity with neurovascular compromise - cold, pale, pulseless foot, call 911
Severe pain with numbness/tingling - possible compartment syndrome or nerve injury
Elderly patients with minimal trauma - possible pathological fracture, needs urgent evaluation
High-energy trauma - possible associated injuries, needs urgent evaluation
